analysis.one_liner: Bans the credit bureaus from charging fees to place, lift, or remove a credit freeze.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was introduced with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it died.
analysis.plain_summary: A credit freeze blocks the credit bureaus from releasing your credit file to anyone opening new credit in your name, which is one of the strongest tools for stopping identity theft. At the time, the bureaus could charge a fee each time a consumer placed, temporarily lifted, or removed a freeze. This bill would make all of those free.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who wants to lock down their credit file to block fraudulent accounts opened in their name. Because freezes were often needed after a data breach, and because people with low incomes were the most likely to skip a paid freeze, waiving the fee helps consumers protect themselves at no cost.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits consumer reporting agencies from charging any fee to place, temporarily lift, or fully remove a credit freeze [S2] [S3].
Requires the bureaus to place a freeze on request, blocking release of a consumer's credit information for new credit without the consumer's permission [S2].
Carves out narrow exceptions so a freeze does not block existing creditors, government agencies acting under legal authority, insurance underwriting, or employers the consumer has authorized [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The consumer reporting agencies — Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — and other credit bureaus, which lose the per-action fees they charged consumers for freezing, lifting, and unfreezing credit files.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies the fee ban only to the large consumer reporting agencies described in section 603(p) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act, so smaller bureaus and specialty reporting companies would not be covered by its fee prohibition [S3].

The freeze itself carries real friction costs for consumers: locking a file means a consumer must lift the freeze before applying for a mortgage, credit card, or phone plan, and the bill does not shorten those processing timelines [S3].
Some states already restricted freeze fees, so the national benefit would have been smaller in those states than the bill's framing suggests [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and modest: consumers get a free, strong identity-theft protection tool instead of paying a fee per action, and the direct cost falls entirely on the credit bureaus' fee revenue. The main honest objection is that a freeze adds a step for consumers who later apply for credit, though the bill keeps exceptions for existing accounts and authorized uses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, so the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Wyden introduced the bill on September 14, 2017, shortly after the Equifax data breach that exposed personal information of over 100 million Americans; a credit freeze was a widely recommended response [S1] [S3] [widely_reported context].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill never advanced beyond committee [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors in the Senate [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The consumer reporting bureaus kept the ability to charge fees for freezes during this Congress. The following year, a broader banking bill made credit freezes free nationwide, so consumers ultimately got the protection through different legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus, until later legislation acted

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban credit freeze fees; it never advanced.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no organized support or opposition on either side.

industries.industry: Consumer credit reporting bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion)
industries.note: The bill eliminates a fee stream the bureaus charged consumers for protecting their own files. The interest runs against consumers: the bureaus' revenue from freeze fees existed because consumers had to pay to restrict access to their own data.
